title: Separation and relaxation for cones of quadratic forms
contribution: A separation algorithm for the cone of quadratic forms over a polyhedral cone, built from optimization over the boundary cone, gives the first separation procedures for 5x5 completely positive matrices and the 4- and 5-dimensional box cones, plus a finite hierarchy of tractable relaxations stronger than the PSD+RLT relaxation.
problem_entry: Nonconvex QP over a pointed polyhedral cone equals linear optimization over C(P) (Theorem 1, p. 6); the standard relaxation D(P) is exact only for n <= 4 (CP) and n <= 3 (box) (p. 5), so the question is how to separate and relax C beyond those dimensions.
key_idea: Separate over C via the dual of the boundary cone C_bd, which splits into lower-dimensional copies of the same cone (Algorithm 1, pp. 9-10); duality gives a nonlinear representation (Proposition 2, p. 12), linearized along step directions d into C(d) and tractable D(d) with C = intersection of C(d) (Propositions 4, 6; Theorem 3, pp. 13-15).
assumptions: Pointed polyhedral cone P with nonempty slice x1 = 1 and nonempty strict interior, the last without loss of generality (Assumptions 1-3, p. 7); optimization over C_bd assumed available (abstract).
proof_devices: Schur-complement lemma for X - xx^T with x = XB^Te (Lemma 2, pp. 8-9)
contradiction via the shift Q + t(A^TA + B^Tee^TB) PSD (Theorem 2, p. 11)
conic strong duality to obtain the nonlinear representation (Proposition 2, p. 12)
smallest step alpha to the boundary to place extreme rays in C(d) (Proposition 4, p. 13)
d chosen as global minimizer of x^TQx on a bounded slice to prove C = intersection of C(d) (Proposition 6, p. 14)
experiments: Illustrative only: Burer-Letchford box-QP instance with 9.29% gap closed by 20 cuts and by D4(d) exactly with Yalmip-CSDP (pp. 27-28); 1,000 random matrices in D4 cap TRI minus C4 with mean normalized distance 0.0022 (p. 28).
positioning: Builds on Sturm-Zhang's cone results and Burer 2009; extends the bad-matrix separation of Burer-Anstreicher-Dur and Dong-Anstreicher to all 5x5 matrices and contrasts its finite hierarchy with Parrilo's (pp. 4-5, 15, 19-20, 27).
writing: Contribution sentences claim firsts ('first separation algorithm for C5', p. 20); open equality stated flatly as unproved in both §3.3 and the future-directions section (pp. 15, 28).
limits_future: Open: whether the intersection of D(d) equals C, relation to Parrilo's hierarchy, adaptive choice of d, computation for large n via small groups (triples) of variables (pp. 15, 28).

method_links.note: QP packaged as linear optimization over one cone C(P); the paper attacks the cone by separation and relaxation
results stated by dimension (n = 5 CP; n = 4, 5 box); proposes applying small separators to triples of variables in large QPs
first test is a literature instance where the standard relaxation leaves a 9.29% gap
open equality printed as open; 'good approximation' backed by 1,000 random samples and called 'some evidence'

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: separation in dimension n reduces to optimization over embedded copies of the dimension n-1 dual cone, so tractability in n-1 yields separation in n

transferable: Separate over a hard generated cone by optimizing over the dual of the cone generated by boundary points; the boundary splits into lower-dimensional copies (pp. 9, 19-20).
Replace a rank-1 nonlinear term by a rank-3 linear term along a step direction and prove exactness of the intersection over all directions (pp. 13-14).

quotes.text: This is the first separation algorithm for C5 and successfully answers the open question as to whether or not C5 is tractable.

title: Unbounded convex sets for non-convex mixed-integer quadratic programming
contribution: Introduces the closures of the convex hulls of lifted mixed-integer quadratic sets, shows every linearly constrained MIQP is linear optimization over a face of one of them, and derives their basic properties, split and psd inequality families, facets and complete descriptions in small dimensions.
problem_entry: Lift MIQP to (x, y = xx^T) and study the hull of feasible pairs; restrict to the unconstrained case, justified because the constrained hull is a face (Proposition 7, p. 11); complications: hull not closed (Proposition 1, p. 5) and never polyhedral (p. 5).
key_idea: Combine polyhedral theory with convex analysis on MIQ and MIQ+ (p. 2); bring MILP/BQP structure into the lifted set: split inequalities from split disjunctions dominate psd inequalities and are facet-inducing for relatively prime v (Proposition 12, Theorems 4-5, pp. 14-15); BQP is a face (Theorem 7, p. 17).
assumptions: Linear equality constraints, nonnegative or free integer and continuous variables, symmetric Q without loss of generality (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: explicit sequence of convex combinations showing non-closedness (Proposition 1, p. 5)
strong NP-hardness via the closest vector problem (Proposition 2, p. 6)
product of disjunct slacks (v^Tx+s)(v^Tx+s+1) >= 0 linearized (Proposition 12, p. 14)
unimodular completion of v for facet proofs (Theorem 5, pp. 14-15)
rank case split with dominance Lemmas 4-5 for the complete description of MIQ_{2,0} (Theorem 8, pp. 22-23)
positioning: Extends Burer-Letchford 2009 box-QP analysis and Padberg/Boros-Hammer BQP inequalities; distinguishes split inequalities from MILP split cuts (pp. 4-5, 14).
writing: Limitation of the unconstrained focus is named as 'a genuine limitation' and immediately answered by the face result (p. 2); open questions collected in the conclusion (pp. 24-25).
limits_future: Complete descriptions only for small (n1, n2) (pp. 21-23); open: fixed-n complexity of MIQ+_{n,0}, non-standard splits, separation of split inequalities (conjectured strongly NP-hard), possibly via psd eigenvector heuristics (pp. 24-25).

method_links.note: one convex object (closure of lifted hull) carries every linearly constrained MIQP via a face
complete linear descriptions pursued in the smallest dimensions where they hold, with the boundary stated
open complexity and a mixed-case facet statement printed as conjectures

transferable: Show the constrained hull is a face of the unconstrained set, so inequalities for the simple set transfer (p. 11).
Derive quadratic valid inequalities from a disjunction by multiplying the two disjunct slacks, then prove dominance over the psd family (p. 14).
Embed a known polytope (BQP) as a face to lift its facets (Theorem 7, Corollary 5, p. 17).

quotes.text: It is our hope that the valid inequalities that we have derived will be used as cutting planes within exact algorithms for non-convex MIQPs, whether constrained or not.
Unfortunately, we conjecture that this problem is strongly NP-hard.

title: MODIFYING SOYSTER'S MODEL FOR THE SYMMETRIC TRAVELING SALESMAN PROBLEM WITH INTERVAL TRAVEL TIMES
contribution: A modified Soyster model for the TSP with interval travel times controls conservatism with one parameter at the cost of a single deterministic TSP, with proven monotone trade-offs and computational comparisons against Soyster, Bertsimas-Sim and robust deviation.
problem_entry: Interval-travel-time TSP: Soyster is cheap but over-conservative, Bertsimas-Sim controls conservatism but needs |E|+1 TSPs, robust deviation needs special algorithms (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Solve one TSP with costs (1-gamma)l + gamma u, gamma in [0,1] read as managerial pessimism (model (8), pp. 12-13); 'balanced' versus Bertsimas-Sim's 'focused' conservatism (p. 13).
assumptions: Symmetric TSP, uncertainty only in objective coefficients, intervals without a natural center (pp. 2, 12).
proof_devices: two-variable LP over the projection of conv(TSP) onto (lower bound, range) (pp. 14-15)
exchange inequalities from optimality at gamma1 < gamma2 (Lemma 1, p. 16) giving Propositions 1-3 (pp. 16-17)
five-node counterexample showing no Bertsimas-Sim analogue (Table 1, pp. 18-19)
experiments: 72 Montemanni et al. iTSP instances from 12 TSPLIB problems, Concorde via MATLAB; single-TSP run times versus up to ~33,000 s for Bertsimas-Sim (Table 2, p. 21); cross-evaluation gaps mostly within 2.13% (Tables 3-4, p. 22); 36 constructed 'somewhat ad hoc' instances with worst-case gaps 11.3% vs 33.9% (pp. 23-24).
positioning: Positions itself between Soyster and Bertsimas-Sim, and against Montemanni et al.'s robust deviation model, the only iTSP-specific method found (pp. 2-4).
writing: Managerial framing of the parameter and a dedicated 'Managerial Insights' section (pp. 3-4, 24-25).
limits_future: Future: asymmetric TSP and edge-specific gamma (p. 25); gamma and Gamma not directly comparable (p. 20).

simple modification of a known model benchmarked against published models with run times first; no theory gap involved

transferable: Project the feasible set onto two objective components (L, R) and derive monotone, ratio-bounded trade-offs from the optimality inequalities at two parameter values (pp. 14-17).
Cross-evaluation table: evaluate each model's optimal solution under the other models' objectives and report percentage gaps (pp. 21-22).

title: A first-order smoothing technique for a class of large-scale linear programs
contribution: Applies Nesterov's primal-dual excessive-gap technique to a class of large dense LPs from machine learning, bounding the unbounded primal set by an upper bound theta on the optimal value and updating theta dynamically to speed convergence, with tests on LP ranking and 1-norm SVMs.
problem_entry: Large dense LPs (LP ranking, 1-norm SVM with kernels) exceed simplex/IPM memory; subgradient is O(1/eps^2) and Mangasarian's Newton is not robust (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Rewrite as nonsmooth (NS0), apply EGT with O(1/eps); bound the domain by c^T alpha <= theta plus Assumption 1.1; complexity scales with theta (Proposition 3.2, p. 8), so update theta online while keeping the excessive-gap condition (Lemma 4.1, Proposition 4.2, Algorithm 5, pp. 12-13).
assumptions: c, w >= 0; Assumption 1.1: known bound on zero-cost alpha components (pp. 2-3), verified for 1-norm SVM (p. 18).
proof_devices: Nesterov's EGT complexity theorem with chosen prox-functions; l1 alternative O(sqrt(m)) worse (Proposition 3.2, p. 8)
intermediate-value argument for existence of theta+ preserving the excessive-gap condition (Lemma 4.1, p. 12)
experiments: 14 UCI ranking datasets vs incremental subgradient (run EGT to eps, then subgradient until it matches or 18,000 s; subgradient matches 5/14, faster in 3), and linear/kernel 1-norm SVMs vs Mangasarian's Newton (faster when it converges, often fails) (pp. 15-21).
positioning: Distinguishes itself from an independent SVM smoothing paper that does not address unboundedness and uses primal-only smoothing (p. 3).
writing: Losses stated with a usage recommendation (subgradient better for quick good solutions, p. 16); conclusion offers the theta-update idea as general (p. 22).
limits_future: Only 1 of 6 hardest kernel instances solved at C = 1 (p. 21); future: theta updating for other nonsmooth problems with unbounded feasible sets (p. 22).

method_links.note: known algorithm (EGT) plus one trick (theta bound and dynamic update), benchmarked against each application's published method with losses printed
test sets are standard application datasets, not a filtered hard pool

transferable: Bound an unbounded domain by an upper bound on the optimal value, make complexity explicit in it, and tighten it online while checking the method's invariant (pp. 3, 12-13).
Comparison protocol without a common stopping rule: run your method to tolerance, then run the baseline until it matches your objective or a time limit (p. 16).
Ablate a parameter update against an oracle best case and a no-update case on one instance (Figure 1, pp. 13-14).

quotes.text: This idea could be extended to other convex nonsmooth problems with unbounded feasible sets.
This observation suggests that the subgradient method might be a better choice if obtaining a good solution in a short time is important.

title: A two-variable approach to the two-trust-region subproblem
contribution: For the two-trust-region subproblem in dimension two, fully characterizes the valid quadratic inequalities (ellipsoid, PSD, vertex RLT and new lifted RLT) that make the SDP relaxation exact, and uses a heuristic lifted-RLT separation for n > 2 to solve 82 of 215 previously unsolved instances.
problem_entry: TTRS is polynomial-time but not via convex relaxation; SDP + SOCRLT still leaves a gap (pp. 2-4); the authors still seek the exact convex relaxation because TTRS appears as a substructure (p. 2).
key_idea: Closing the gap = describing the cone K of quadratics valid on the intersection (Proposition 2.1, p. 5); for n = 2 show every valid quadratic is minorized by one in G (Proposition 2.2, Theorem 4.3, pp. 5, 14-15), where G adds 'lifted RLT' quadratics T_yE1 T_zE2 + lambda L_yz^2 (Table 1, pp. 6-7).
assumptions: n = 2 for the theory; full-dimensional intersection, no containment, independent gradients at vertices (simplifying, p. 3).
proof_devices: minorization implies the generating family contains all extreme rays (Proposition 2.2, p. 5)
break (order of first nonzero boundary derivative), parameterization-independent via Faa di Bruno (Proposition 3.1, pp. 8-9)
perturbation f + lambda g valid for some lambda < 0 when zeros and breaks are dominated (Lemma 4.1, pp. 13-14)
even break at nonvertex zeros (Lemma 4.2, p. 14) and case analysis (Theorem 4.3, pp. 14-15)
experiments: n = 2 instance with 2.74% SOCRLT gap closed by one cut, 2013 example closed after six cuts; on the 215 instances from Burer-Anstreicher 2013 unsolved by SOCRLT (n = 5, 10, 20; solved = relative gap < 1e-4) 82 solved, at more than 10x CPU time; solver change disclosed (pp. 19-20).
positioning: Strengthens Burer-Anstreicher 2013 SOCRLT; acknowledges Bienstock's polynomial algorithm and contrasts it as non-relaxation-based (p. 2).
writing: Main theorem previewed early with a table of generators and nicknames (pp. 3, 6); open n > 2 question stated as uncertainty ('We are unsure', p. 18).
limits_future: Theory only for n = 2; exactness of lifted RLT for n > 2 unknown (p. 18); 133 of 215 hard instances unsolved and cuts are costly (pp. 19-20).

method_links.note: small substructure (two ellipsoids), SDP+SOCRLT kitchen sink as reference, strictly stronger family, proof in n = 2 and heuristic beyond
hard pool = the 2013 paper's unsolved instances (41+70+104 = 215), solved criterion restated, solver change disclosed
n > 2 extension labelled heuristic and exactness left open

transferable: Prove a relaxation exact by showing every valid inequality dominates one in your generating family (pp. 5, 14-15).
Track the order of contact ('break') at zeros of a valid quadratic to decide when it can be perturbed by another valid quadratic (pp. 8, 13-14).
Seed separation of a new cut family with support points returned by an existing cheaper separation routine (p. 17).

quotes.text: We believe it is still interesting to seek the convex relaxation that solves TTRS exactly.
Applying our heuristic lifted-RLT constraints to the 215 previously unsolved instances, we can solve 82—about 38%—of them; see Table 3.

title: Nearly-efficient tuitions and subsidies in American public higher education
contribution: A two-stage legislature-university model shows optimal unrestricted enrollment subsidies are proportional to maximum net willingness to pay (Ramsey subsidies), reduces the legislature's problem to a one-dimensional convex program, and calibrates restricted-subsidy scenarios to Iowa and Michigan budgets.
problem_entry: Why do public universities keep inefficient cross-subsidies (p. 1)? Prior empirical work treats subsidies as exogenous; here tuitions and subsidies are jointly determined (p. 2).
key_idea: Leader-follower model with the university's closed-form quasi-efficient enrollment rule substituted (pp. 3-5); k-ratio subsidies (Result 2, p. 5) and reduction to a 1-D strictly convex program (Result 3, p. 5).
assumptions: Linear demand, constant marginal costs, linear enrollment subsidies, stated as restrictive and chosen for closed forms (p. 2); positivity and break-even feasibility conditions (p. 3).
proof_devices: efficiency scalar forced once the follower's rule is imposed (Result 1, pp. 12-13)
KKT conditions of the restriction with rho fixed give s_ij = k d_ij (Result 2, p. 13)
change of variables x = rho(1+k) to a one-dimensional strictly convex program (Result 3, pp. 13-14)
experiments: Calibration to FY2014 decentralized budgets of University of Iowa and University of Michigan under three subsidy scenarios; efficiency gains of 8% (UI) and 4% (UM) with large resident-to-nonresident redistribution (pp. 2-3, 6-7).
positioning: Extends Baumol-Bradford Ramsey pricing to endogenous appropriations; builds on Fethke's earlier tuition models (pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: Policy-economics register with long footnotes on institutional practice; restrictive assumptions announced up front (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: Restricted subsidy cases need iterative numerical solution (p. 6); increasing marginal cost not calibrated (p. 6); conclusion: equity may trump efficiency (p. 12).

method_links.note: exact reformulation by change of variables turns the two-stage problem into a one-dimensional strictly convex program, but no cone is involved

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: calibrate a stylized model to institutional data
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: closed-form model results checked by replicating real university budget allocations and quantifying welfare losses

transferable: In a leader-follower model with a closed-form follower optimum, substitute it as a constraint, fix the troublesome scalar, read the leader's structure from KKT, then remove the scalar by a product change of variables (pp. 12-14).

quotes.text: Our formulations are restrictive in their specification of linear demand curves, constant marginal costs, and linear enrollment subsides.
Our numerical results for these public universities suggest that equity may trump efficiency in determining actual subsidies.

title: How to convexify the intersection of a second order cone and a nonconvex quadratic
contribution: Under easy-to-check conditions, aggregating an SOC-representable cone with a nonconvex homogeneous quadratic up to the first singular point of the matrix pencil gives a computable SOC-representable relaxation that equals the closed conic (and, for cross-sections, convex) hull under further conditions, unifying split and two-term disjunction results and covering TRS.
problem_entry: Multiple papers proved conv(ellipsoid cap split disjunction) is SOCr with different techniques (pp. 2-3); generalize to any single homogeneous quadratic, without rank <= 2 or convex-complement assumptions (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Conic aggregation (1-t)f0 + t f1 requiring convexity only on {f0 <= 0}; s = first t with A_t singular; cl.conic.hull(F0+ cap F1) contained in F0+ cap Fs+, equal under Condition 4, cross-section version under Condition 5 (Theorem 1, pp. 3, 7-8).
assumptions: Conditions 1-3 (one negative eigenvalue of A0, full dimensionality, nonsingularity or definiteness on null(A0)); Condition 4 regularity; Condition 5 for cross-sections (pp. 7-8); all checkable by eigen-decompositions and a two-constraint SDP (pp. 4, 9).
proof_devices: containment chain F0+ cap F1 within F0+ cap Fs+ within conic.hull(F0+ cap F1) (pp. 12-13)
Rellich's analytic perturbation theorem for eigenvalues along the pencil A_t (Theorem 2, p. 14; details not read)
experiments: n/a (low-dimensional illustrative examples, pp. 10-12 and Online Supplement pp. 34-39, not read in detail)
positioning: Unifies Gunluk-Linderoth, Dadush et al., Modaresi et al., Andersen-Jensen, Belotti et al., Kilinc-Karzan-Yildiz and Bienstock-Michalka on SOC disjunctions; notes that these convexify in original variables, unlike lifted-space QP approaches (pp. 2-4).
writing: Explicit contrast paragraph with each prior line; validity and sufficiency conditions separated; disclaimer that TRS-by-SOCP is not proposed as a numerical method (pp. 3-4, 27).
limits_future: Future: pair each nonconvex quadratic with an ellipsoid in general QCQPs; multiple cones or quadratics; notes a later similar aggregation paper relying on numerical algorithms (pp. 30-31).

method_links.note: small substructure (one SOC and one quadratic) with an explicit compact SOC description of the hull instead of a disjunctive formulation
step 4 unification: known disjunction cases recovered by one object
TRS section states what is not claimed

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: conditions guaranteeing a valid relaxation are stated apart from conditions guaranteeing exactness, so partial hypotheses still yield cuts

transferable: Aggregate a convex and a nonconvex quadratic with weight t and stop at the first singular point of the pencil to get a valid SOCr set (pp. 7-8).
State conditions for validity separately from conditions for exactness (p. 4).
Provide pseudocode to verify the hypotheses and compute the cut so the theorem is usable as an algorithm (pp. 4, 9).

quotes.text: Another useful feature of our approach is that we clearly distinguish the conditions guaranteeing validity of our relaxation from those ensuring sufficiency.

title: Robust sensitivity analysis of the optimal value of linear programming
contribution: Defines best- and worst-case LP optimal values under simultaneous perturbations of objective and right-hand side in a compact convex set, reformulates them exactly as copositive programs, and bounds them with SDP relaxations using RLT, SOC-RLT and a redundant complementarity constraint, validated on literature examples.
problem_entry: Classical sensitivity analysis handles single or interval changes; general simultaneous perturbations lead to NP-hard nonconvex QPs and had not been studied (p. 2); closest is Peng-Zhu worst-case LP with ellipsoidal b (p. 3).
key_idea: Bilinear QPs for p-, p+ with finite variants q-, q+ (p. 4); exact generalized copositive reformulation over hom(U) x cones (Theorem 1, p. 13); SDP relaxations with RLT/SOC-RLT from U and linearized x∘s = 0 (pp. 12-14).
assumptions: U compact convex containing (0,0) (Assumption 1, p. 6); nominal primal and dual feasible sets nonempty, one bounded (Assumption 2, p. 10); only (b, c) perturbed and only the optimal value studied (p. 4).
proof_devices: embedding the bilinear QPs into the general form of Burer's copositive equivalence lemma (Lemma 1, Theorem 1, pp. 12-13)
products of pairs of linear constraints of R+ x K linearized as valid constraints (pp. 13-14)
experiments: Six literature examples plus a network flow problem, Python + Mosek at defaults (p. 16); two-sided certification via translated SDP solutions with alternating local improvement and a 10,000-point extreme-point sampler (pp. 15-16); systemic-risk table limited to 10 instances without Mosek numerical issues (p. 21); 0.2% gaps remain in two SOC network cases (p. 24); linearized complementarity changes q+ by up to 1671% (p. 24).
positioning: Generalizes Peng-Zhu (both b and c, general U, best and worst case) and connects to two-stage adaptive optimization; says it is not robust optimization (pp. 3-5).
writing: Explicit list of caveats in the introduction (pp. 4-5); claims of being first stated with the lack of comparators (p. 23).
limits_future: Value only, not solution; constraint-matrix perturbations and speed of the largest relaxations left for future work (pp. 4, 25).

method_links.note: a new question is packaged exactly as a copositive program and then attacked by tractable SDP relaxations
two-sided signal (relaxation vs feasible bounds) used, but 'no gap for all tested examples' stated beside 0.2% gaps
filter disclosed, but it removes instances hard for the solver/method rather than selecting the baseline's failures

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: add a redundant nonconvex constraint (complementary slackness) to the exact model because its linearization tightens the relaxation; measured by ablation

transferable: Two-sided certification of a relaxation bound: feasible points from the relaxation's solution improved by alternating convex solves, plus a random-extreme-point sampler (pp. 15-16).
Ablate each added constraint class with a 'without it' table (Table 5, p. 24).
Add redundant complementarity constraints before relaxing (pp. 12, 23-24).

quotes.text: First, we focus only on how the optimal value is affected by uncertainty, not the optimal solution.
As ours is the first approach to study general perturbations in the literature, we are aware of no existing methods for this problem with which to compare our results.
